title: Agentic AI Oversight: Governing Rogue AI Agents
summary: Agentic AI oversight explained: where shadow AI agents come from, how to tier them by data sensitivity and autonomy, and why deterministic controls come before model security.
body_markdown:
*Last updated: November 2026*


**TL;DR:**


- [Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/agentic-ai-oversight) named agentic AI oversight a Top Trend in Cybersecurity for 2026: AI adoption is outpacing the ability to govern it.
- Shadow AI agents arrive three ways: embedded in software you already approved, taken directly from the internet, or built by employees.
- Gartner reports 75% of organisations seeing unauthorised use of AI coding assistants, and 50% reporting employee access to public SaaS GenAI agent platforms.
- Tier agents on two axes, data sensitivity and autonomy. Not all agents carry the same risk.
- Deterministic controls first, model security second. Only one of them is auditable.


## Why oversight is behind


Agents are not bought the way software is bought. They appear inside tools that were already approved, they are picked up directly from the internet, and increasingly they are written by employees who are not developers. None of those paths crosses procurement, so none of them produces the paperwork a security programme is built to consume.


[Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/agentic-ai-oversight) puts numbers on how common this already is: **75% of organisations report unauthorised use of AI coding assistants** , and **50% report employee access to public SaaS GenAI agent platforms** . Among senior cybersecurity professionals, **61% have observed AI agent automation inside existing approved enterprise software** , and **59% suspect or have evidence of unsanctioned employee use** .


That third statistic is the uncomfortable one. It is not about staff going around IT. It is about agent capability arriving in an update to software that was already signed off, which means an approved-vendor list offers no protection at all.


## ✨ The three places shadow AI agents come from


Source What it looks like Why discovery misses it


Embedded in approved software An agent feature switched on inside a SaaS tool already on your list. The vendor passed review. Nothing new appears in the inventory, and the capability arrived in a release note.


Taken directly from the internet A public GenAI agent platform someone signs into with a work email. No procurement, no SSO, often a personal account. Invisible unless you are watching the endpoint or the browser.


Built by employees A no-code automation or something assembled through vibe coding. It is not a product, so there is no vendor to review. It runs on a laptop or in a workflow tool.


The practical consequence is that a discovery approach built on vendor relationships finds roughly none of these. What finds them is presence where the agents actually run, which for the first and third categories is the endpoint.[MCP server discovery](https://www.strac.io/blog/mcp-server-discovery) covers one half of that and[shadow AI detection](https://www.strac.io/blog/shadow-ai-detection-tools) covers the other.


## ✨ Not every AI agent carries the same risk


The instinct when agents start appearing is to apply one oversight process to all of them. That fails in both directions: it is too heavy for the harmless majority and too light for the few that matter.


[Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/agentic-ai-oversight) , which named agentic AI oversight a Top Trend in Cybersecurity for 2026, frames this as two axes rather than one: the sensitivity of the data an agent can access, and its level of autonomy, which they define as agency plus automation. Most programmes measure only the first, and that is why they end up treating a read-only summariser and an autonomous coding agent as the same object.


### Why autonomy is the axis people miss


Data sensitivity is familiar territory: every security team already classifies data. Autonomy is newer and harder to see. An agent that drafts a reply for a human to send is bounded by that human. One that reads a repository, decides what to change and opens a pull request is not. The same data access carries very different consequences across those two, and nothing in a data classification scheme captures the difference.


Tier agents on both axes. An agent with broad data access and no human in the loop is a different problem from one with either alone.


### What to do in each quadrant


Data the agent can reach Autonomy The control that fits


Low sensitivity Low Audit only. Enforcement here costs goodwill and prevents almost nothing.


Low sensitivity High Watch behaviour. The data is dull, the blast radius is not, and scope tends to grow quietly.


Sensitive Low Inspect content in both directions: what the agent is given, and what it returns.


Sensitive High The top tier. Allowlist the server, block at tool level, and keep a per-agent audit trail.


Gartner's recommendation is to build an AI agent risk profile, document each agent's permissions and scope, and categorise agents by business risk, rather than applying one level of oversight to all of them. In practice the inputs to that profile are concrete: which server the agent connects through, which tools that server exposes, what paths it is allowed, and which client is driving it. See[MCP server discovery](https://www.strac.io/blog/mcp-server-discovery) for where those come from.


### Deterministic controls before model controls


One more point from the same article is worth stating plainly because it decides sequencing: implement deterministic controls first and complement them with model security, not the other way round. A rule that blocks a specific tool, or redacts a specific data class, behaves the same way every time. A model-layer guardrail is probabilistic. Both have a place, and only one of them can be audited.


## Rogue automation changes incident response


Most incident response processes assume a human on the other end, acting at human speed, through an account you can disable. An agent breaks all three assumptions. It acts in bursts, it may be running under a service identity rather than a person, and disabling the account it borrows can take down legitimate work alongside it.


Gartner is explicit that response processes need upgrading to stand a chance of discovering and mitigating rogue AI automations. In practice that means three things an IR runbook rarely has today: the ability to attribute an action to a specific agent rather than an account, the ability to revoke one agent's access without revoking the person's, and a record of what the agent actually reached rather than what it was permitted to reach.


## 🎥 What oversight looks like when it is working


Discovery, tiering, enforcement and evidence as one workflow rather than four tools.


## Where to start


Gartner's advice is to pace investment and focus early effort on data security and access management, which is a usefully narrow starting point. Concretely: inventory what is running, including MCP servers and coding agents; tier what you find on the two axes above; put deterministic controls on the top tier only; and leave everything else in audit until the data tells you otherwise.


The common failure is the opposite order, starting with a policy document and a blanket restriction. That produces a programme engineering routes around in a fortnight.[AI agent security platforms](https://www.strac.io/blog/best-ai-agent-security-platforms) covers how to score vendors against this, and[blocking MCP connectors](https://www.strac.io/blog/block-mcp-connectors) covers enforcement at tool level.


## 🌶️ Spicy FAQs on agentic AI oversight


### What is agentic AI oversight?


It is the practice of knowing which AI agents are operating in your organisation, what each can reach, how much it can do without a human, and being able to act on that. Gartner named it a Top Trend in Cybersecurity for 2026 on the basis that AI adoption is expanding faster than most organisations can govern it.


### What is a rogue AI agent?


An agent operating outside formal oversight. It is rarely malicious. The common cases are an automation someone built with a no-code tool, an agent feature switched on inside software your organisation already approved, or a coding assistant an engineer installed to work faster. None of those arrive through procurement, and none appear in a SaaS inventory.


### Where do shadow AI agents actually come from?


Gartner names three sources: agents embedded in existing enterprise software, agents consumed directly from the internet, and agents employees build themselves, including through vibe coding. The first is the one most programmes miss entirely, because the software was already approved and the agent capability arrived in an update nobody reviewed.


### How do you tier AI agents by risk?


On two axes: the sensitivity of the data the agent can access, and its level of autonomy. An agent with broad data access and no human in the loop needs tool-level enforcement and a per-agent audit trail. One with narrow access and a human approving each step needs little more than audit. Treating them identically is how oversight programmes become unaffordable and get abandoned.


### What is a track-back inventory?


An indirect way to find agents you cannot discover head-on. Rather than enumerating agents, you watch for changes in how your sensitive APIs are being used, and work backwards from an unusual pattern to whatever is driving it. Gartner suggests it precisely because direct discovery will not keep pace with how fast agents appear.


### Why are deterministic controls recommended before model security?


Because they are predictable and auditable. A rule that blocks a named tool, or redacts a named data class, produces the same outcome every time and leaves a record. Model-layer guardrails are probabilistic and much harder to evidence to an auditor. The sequence matters: get the deterministic layer in place, then add model controls on top.


### How does incident response change for rogue automations?


The volume and the speed both change. A human insider acts at human pace; an agent can touch thousands of records before anyone opens a ticket. Response processes built around a person need to be able to identify which agent acted, on whose authority, and revoke that specific agent's access rather than disabling an account.
